story: Deucalion was the son of the Titan Prometheus, and ruled over a region called Phthia. Zeus, the king of the gods, grew angry at humanity's wickedness after King Lycaon sacrificed a boy to him, and decided to destroy the Bronze Age of mankind with a great flood. Prometheus forewarned his son Deucalion of the coming deluge, so Deucalion built a wooden chest and provisioned it carefully; no animals were saved in this version. He and his wife Pyrrha, daughter of the Titan Epimetheus, entered the chest together. The rivers ran in torrents and the sea flooded the coastal plains until, after nine days, the waters receded and the chest came to rest on a mountain. Once safe, the couple gave thanks to Zeus. Deucalion then consulted an oracle of the goddess Themis about how to repopulate the earth, and was told to cover his head and throw the bones of his mother behind his shoulder. The couple understood that 'mother' meant Gaia, the earth itself, and 'bones' meant stones. As they walked, they threw stones behind their shoulders: those thrown by Deucalion became men, and those thrown by Pyrrha became women. These new people were called the Leleges, and they settled the region of Locris. Deucalion and Pyrrha also had children of their own, including a son named Hellen, ancestor of a people who ruled Thessaly, and daughters. One daughter, by the sea god Poseidon, became mother of Delphus, founder of a city. Deucalion later fled his kingdom with his sons to Athens, where he built a sanctuary to Zeus and eventually died and was buried.
